sections.title: Introduction
claims: The question: given a fixed FLOPs budget, how to trade off model size and training tokens (Eq. 1).
Kaplan et al. (2020) would grow the model 5.5x and the data 1.8x for 10x compute; this paper finds equal proportions.
Current large models (Table 1) are trained for approximately 300 billion tokens.
Prediction: for Gopher's budget, an optimal model is 4 times smaller trained on 4 times more tokens; Chinchilla = 70B on 1.4T tokens.

sections.title: Related work: modelling the scaling behavior
claims: Difference 1 from Kaplan: Kaplan fixed training tokens and the LR schedule for all models; intermediate losses of a fixed cosine-to-130B schedule overestimate the loss of a model trained with a matched schedule.
Difference 2: models up to 16B, majority over 500M parameters, versus Kaplan's majority under 100M; slight curvature in the FLOP-loss frontier (Appendix E).

sections.title: Estimating the optimal allocation (three approaches)
claims: All three approaches assume a power-law relationship between compute and model size.
All predict parameter count and tokens should be increased equally with compute (Table 2).

sections.title: Approach 1: fix model sizes, vary training tokens
claims: Model family 70M to over 10B; each size trained for 4 horizons spanning 16x, LR decayed 10x by cosine over each horizon.
Smooth and interpolate each curve; at 1500 log-spaced FLOP values take the run with lowest loss (the envelope); fit N_opt ~ C^a, D_opt ~ C^b with a = 0.50, b = 0.50.
Footnote 4: all selected points lie within the last 15% of training, so the cosine cycle should decay 10x over approximately D tokens.

sections.title: Approach 2: IsoFLOP profiles
claims: 9 FLOP budgets from 6e18 to 3e21; vary model size (up to 16B), tokens fixed by the budget; final loss only.
Fit a parabola to each IsoFLOP curve to locate the loss-minimising model size; then power laws give a = 0.49, b = 0.51.

sections.title: Approach 3: parametric loss
claims: L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta (Eq. 2): entropy of text, finite-capacity term, finite-training term.
Fit by Huber loss (delta = 1e-3) on log loss with L-BFGS from a grid of initialisations (Eq. 3).
Minimising under FLOPs ~ 6ND gives the closed form Eq. 4: a = beta/(alpha+beta), b = alpha/(alpha+beta); a = 0.46, b = 0.54.
Projected optimal size for the Gopher budget: 40B parameters (Fig. 4 caption).

sections.title: Optimal model scaling
claims: Approach 3 predicts even smaller models at large budgets: Huber down-weights low-FLOP points and the frontier has negative curvature.
Table 3 (Approach 1 projections): 1B -> 20.2B tokens, 10B -> 205.1B, 67B -> 1.5T, 280B -> 5.9T; the prose gives 175B -> 4.41e24 FLOPs and over 4.2T tokens, 280B -> ~1e25 FLOPs and 6.8T tokens.
A 1T model is unlikely to be optimal below 1e26 FLOPs (over 250x Gopher).
C4 and GitHub IsoFLOP replications reach the same equal-scaling conclusion (Appendix C, Table A2).

sections.title: Chinchilla
claims: Optimal size for Gopher's budget estimated between 40 and 70 billion; chose 70B for 1.4T tokens.
Same FLOPs as Gopher; 4x smaller so memory footprint and inference cost are smaller.
Differences from Gopher (4.1): MassiveText subset distribution, AdamW instead of Adam, modified SentencePiece tokenizer without NFKC, float32 weight copy in optimiser state.

sections.title: Results
claims: The Pile: Chinchilla beats Gopher on all subsets; Wikitext103 perplexity 7.16 vs 7.75; leakage caveat since Chinchilla saw 4x more data.
MMLU 5-shot: 67.6% vs Gopher 60.0% (abstract says 67.5%); better on 51/57 tasks, same on 2, worse on 4.
BIG-bench: better than Gopher on all but four tasks.

sections.title: Discussion and limitations
claims: Limitation 1: only two comparable large-scale runs (Chinchilla and Gopher), no intermediate-scale tests.
Limitation 2: assumes a power-law frontier but observes concavity in log(N_opt) at high compute (Appendix E) so optimal sizes may still be overestimated.
Limitation 3: all runs are under one epoch of data.
Call for dataset scaling with attention to quality, leakage, toxicity and privacy.

sections.title: Appendix B: optimal cosine cycle length
claims: 10x LR decay; cycle length too much longer than the training steps hurts; overshooting by more than 25% gives clear drops (Fig. A1).

sections.title: Appendix D.2: parametric fitting
claims: Risk decomposition Eq. 9: Bayes risk + function-approximation term + stochastic-approximation term.
Fitted Eq. 10: L = E + A/N^0.34 + B/D^0.28 with E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7; both exponents below 1/2.
Eq. 11 fits a, b, e, alpha, beta via LSE on log scale; grid of initialisations; delta = 1e-3.

sections.title: Appendix D.3: frontier for Approaches 2 and 3 (Table A3)
claims: Approach 2: 1B -> 20.0B tokens, 10B -> 219.5B; Approach 3: 1B -> 27.1B, 10B -> 410.1B, 67B -> 4.1T.

sections.title: Appendix D.4: head-to-head vs Kaplan at 1e21 FLOPs
claims: Kaplan predicts 4.68B optimal, Approach 1 predicts 2.86B; trained 4.74B and 2.80B models; the 2.80B model wins (Fig. A4).

sections.title: Appendix E: curvature of the FLOP-loss frontier
claims: Fits to the first, middle and last third of frontier points differ (Fig. A5); curvature suggests even smaller models may be optimal at large budgets.

sections.title: Appendix F: FLOPs computation
claims: Embedding FLOPs and parameters are counted; factor 2 per multiply-accumulate; backward = 2x forward; Table A4 ratio of exact FLOPs to 6ND ranges 0.99-1.10, 'very small'.
Gopher's budget is 6.3e23 with this calculation vs 5.76e23 in Rae et al.

sections.title: Appendix G: other Chinchilla/Gopher differences
claims: AdamW beats Adam independent of LR schedule (Figs. A6, A7); higher-precision optimiser weight copy.

tables.caption: Table 1: Current LLMs. We show five of the current largest dense transformer models, their size, and the number of training tokens. Other than LaMDA (Thoppilan et al., 2022), most models are trained for approximately 300 billion tokens. We introduce Chinchilla, a substantially smaller model, trained for much longer than 300B tokens.

Table 2: Estimated parameter and data scaling with increased training compute. The listed values are the exponents, $a$ and $b$ , on the relationship $N_{opt}\propto C^{a}$ and $D_{opt}\propto C^{b}$ . Our analysis suggests a near equal scaling in parameters and data with increasing compute which is in clear contrast to previous work on the scaling of large models. The 10 ${}^{\text{th}}$ and 90 ${}^{\text{th}}$ percentiles are estimated via bootstrapping data (80% of the dataset is sampled 100 times) and are shown in parenthesis.

Table 3: Estimated optimal training FLOPs and training tokens for various model sizes. For various model sizes, we show the projections from Approach 1 of how many FLOPs and training tokens would be needed to train compute-optimal models. The estimates for Approach 2 & 3 are similar (shown in Section D.3) .

Table 4: Chinchilla architecture details. We list the number of layers, the key/value size, the bottleneck activation size d ${}_{\text{model}}$ , the maximum learning rate, and the training batch size (# tokens). The feed-forward size is always set to $4\times\textrm{d}_{\textrm{model}}$ . Note that we double the batch size midway through training for both Chinchilla and Gopher. In Appendix G we show the impact of the various optimiser related changes between Chinchilla and Gopher. All models in this analysis have been trained on TPUv3/TPUv4 (Jouppi et al., 2017) with JAX (Bradbury et al., 20

Table 5: All evaluation tasks. We evaluate Chinchilla on a collection of language modelling along with downstream tasks. We evaluate on largely the same tasks as in Rae et al. (2021), to allow for direct comparison.

tables.caption: Table 6: Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU). We report the average 5-shot accuracy over 57 tasks with model and human accuracy comparisons taken from Hendrycks et al. (2020). We also include the average prediction for state of the art accuracy in June 2022/2023 made by 73 competitive human forecasters in Steinhardt (2021).

Table 7: Reading comprehension. On RACE-h and RACE-m (Lai et al., 2017), Chinchilla considerably improves performance over Gopher. Note that GPT-3 and MT-NLG 530B use a different prompt format than we do on RACE-h/m, so results are not comparable to Gopher and Chinchilla. On LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016), Chinchilla outperforms both Gopher and MT-NLG 530B.

Table 8: Zero-shot comparison on Common Sense benchmarks. We show a comparison between Chinchilla, Gopher, and MT-NLG 530B on various Common Sense benchmarks. We see that Chinchilla matches or outperforms Gopher and GPT-3 on all tasks. On all but one Chinchilla outperforms the much larger MT-NLG 530B model. We evaluate Chinchilla on various common sense benchmarks: PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), SIQA (Sap et al., 2019), Winogrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019).

Table 9: Closed-book question answering. For Natural Questions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), Chinchilla outperforms Gopher in all cases. On Natural Questions, Chinchilla outperforms GPT-3. On TriviaQA we show results on two different evaluation sets to allow for comparison to GPT-3 and to open book SOTA (FiD + Distillation (Izacard and Grave, 2020)).

Table 10: Winogender results. Left: Chinchilla consistently resolves pronouns better than Gopher. Right: Chinchilla performs better on examples which contradict gender stereotypes (gotcha examples). However, difference in performance across groups suggests Chinchilla exhibits bias.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overlaid predictions. We overlay the predictions from our three different approaches, along with projections from Kaplan et al. (2020). We find that all three methods predict that current large models should be substantially smaller and therefore trained much longer than is currently done. In Figure A3, we show the results with the predicted optimal tokens plotted against the optimal number of parameters for fixed FLOP budgets. Chinchilla outperforms Gopher and the other large models (see Section 4.2).

Figure 2: Training curve envelope. On the left we show all of our different runs. We launched a range of model sizes going from 70M to 10B, each for four different cosine cycle lengths. From these curves, we extracted the envelope of minimal loss per FLOP, and we used these points to estimate the optimal model size (center) for a given compute budget and the optimal number of training tokens (right). In green, we show projections of optimal model size and training token count based on the number of FLOPs used to train Gopher ( $5.76\times 10^{23}$ ). For each parameter count $N$ we train 4 dif

Figure 3: IsoFLOP curves. For various model sizes, we choose the number of training tokens such that the final FLOPs is a constant. The cosine cycle length is set to match the target FLOP count. We find a clear valley in loss, meaning that for a given FLOP budget there is an optimal model to train (left). Using the location of these valleys, we project optimal model size and number of tokens for larger models (center and right). In green, we show the estimated number of parameters and tokens for an optimal model trained with the compute budget of Gopher.

Figure 4: Parametric fit. We fit a parametric modelling of the loss $\hat{L}(N,D)$ and display contour (left) and isoFLOP slices (right). For each isoFLOP slice, we include a corresponding dashed line in the left plot. In the left plot, we show the efficient frontier in blue, which is a line in log-log space. Specifically, the curve goes through each iso-loss contour at the point with the fewest FLOPs.

Figure 5: Pile Evaluation. For the different evaluation sets in The Pile (Gao et al., 2020), we show the bits-per-byte (bpb) improvement (decrease) of Chinchilla compared to Gopher. On all subsets, Chinchilla outperforms Gopher. Chinchilla significantly outperforms Gopher on all evaluation subsets of The Pile (Gao et al., 2020), as shown in Figure 5.

Figure 6: MMLU results compared to Gopher We find that Chinchilla outperforms Gopher by 7.6% on average (see Table 6) in addition to performing better on 51/57 individual tasks, the same on 2/57, and worse on only 4/57 tasks.
Figure 7: BIG-bench results compared to Gopher Chinchilla out performs Gopher on all but four BIG-bench tasks considered. Full results are in Table A7.

Figure A1: Grid over cosine cycle length. We show 6 curves with the cosine cycle length set to 1, 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, and 5 $\times$ longer than the target number of training steps. When the cosine cycle length is too long, and the learning rate does not drop appropriately, then performance is impaired. We find that overestimating the number of training steps beyond 25% leads to clear drops in performance. We show results where we have set the number of training steps to two different values (top and bottom).

Figure A2: C4 and GitHub IsoFLOP curves. Using the C4 dataset (Raffel et al., 2020b) and a GitHub dataset (Rae et al., 2021), we generate 4 IsoFLOP profiles and show the parameter and token count scaling, as in Figure 3. Scaling coefficients are shown in Table A2. We show scaling results from an IsoFLOP (Approach 2) analysis after training on two different datasets: C4 (Raffel et al., 2020b) and GitHub code (we show results with data from Rae et al. (2021)), results are shown in Table A2.

Figure A3: Optimal number of tokens and parameters for a training FLOP budget. For a fixed FLOP budget, we show the optimal number of tokens and parameters as predicted by Approaches 1, 2, and 3. For an alternate representation, see Figure 1.

Figure A4: Comparison to Kaplan et al. (2020) at $10^{21}$ FLOPs. We train 2.80 and 4.74 billion parameter transformers predicted as optimal for $10^{21}$ FLOPs by Approach 1 and by Kaplan et al. (2020). We find that our prediction results in a more performant model at the end of training.

Figure A5: Training curve envelopes. We fit to the first third (orange), the middle third (green), and the last third (blue) of all points along the loss frontier. We plot only a subset of the points.

Figure A6: Comparison of other differences. Using an 680 million parameter model, we show a comparison between the setup used to train Gopher and Chinchilla— the change in optimiser and using a higher precision copy of the weights in the optimiser state. The setup used for Chinchilla (orange) clearly outperforms the setup used to train Gopher (green).

Figure A7: Adam vs AdamW. For a 417M (blue) and 1.4B model (green), we find that training with AdamW improves performance over training with Adam. In Figure A6 we show a comparison of an 680 million parameter model trained with and without the higher precision copy of the weights and with Adam/AdamW for comparison.

findings.question: How should N and D grow with C?
findings.metric: exponents a, b of N_opt ~ C^a, D_opt ~ C^b

findings.question: How many tokens for a given model size?
findings.takeaway: Approach 1: 1B -> 20.2B tokens, 10B -> 205.1B, 67B -> 1.5T (roughly 20 tokens per parameter; the phrase itself is not printed in the paper).

findings.question: Does a 4x smaller model on 4x more data beat Gopher at equal FLOPs?
findings.metric: Pile bpb, Wikitext103 ppl, MMLU, BIG-bench
findings.takeaway: Yes on nearly every task: Wikitext103 7.16 vs 7.75, MMLU 67.6% vs 60.0%, 51/57 MMLU tasks better.

findings.question: Is the disagreement with Kaplan real at small scale?
findings.takeaway: The 2.80B model (this paper's prediction) beats the 4.74B model (Kaplan's).

findings.question: Does the LR schedule length matter for the fits?
findings.takeaway: Overshooting the training horizon by more than 25% clearly degrades loss; the schedule must match D.

findings.question: Do exponents depend on the dataset?
findings.metric: a, b on C4 and GitHub
